name: Favorlang
confidence_why: The only evidence is Jacobus Vertrecht's own note of about 1650, printed in Campbell 1896, that his acute marks a syllable pronounced 'hard and long', and in his text the mark falls on final, penultimate and antepenultimate syllables in different words, so whether Favorlang had word stress at all, and where, remains a guess; every other work consulted (Happart 1650, Li 2003, Li 2004, Blust 2013, Joby 2026) says nothing about it.

The articles of Christian instruction in Favorlang-Formosan, Dutch and English, from Vertrecht's manuscript of 1650; with Psalmanazar's Dialogue between a Japanese and a Formosan, and Happart's Favorlang vocabulary. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner & Co. (Preface fn. reproduces Jacobus Vertrecht's c.1650 note on his accent marks.)
catalog_locator: Preface p. xiv, footnote 1 (cu31924026424675); accent placement checked on text p. 8

new_statements.quote: ... the sentences were numbered to facilitate reference, and all accents filled in as they occur in the original manuscript.[1] ... [fn. 1] As much may depend on the somewhat peculiar use made of those accents, the following is a copy of the author's own note on the subject:— 'Waar boven de syllabe een schuinsche linie (') staat, dat die hard en lang moet uitgesprookken werden; desgeliks boven de g een liggende linie, aldus (g) wyst aan die hard tegen de syde van de strot word uitgesprookken; en waar onder s op dese wyse een comma staat (ş) geeft te kennen, dat d'selve fast en light word uitgesprookken als een c.'
new_statements.translation: [Vertrecht's note:] 'Where an oblique stroke (') stands above the syllable, [it indicates] that it must be pronounced hard and long; likewise a horizontal line over the g, thus (g), shows that it is pronounced hard against the side of the throat; and where a comma stands under s in this way (ş) it indicates that it is pronounced fast and light like a c.'
new_statements.citation: Vertrecht, Jacobus (c. 1650), author's note on his orthography, quoted in: Campbell, William (ed.) 1896. The articles of Christian instruction in Favorlang-Formosan, Dutch and English, from Vertrecht's manuscript of 1650. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Truebner & Co.
new_statements.locator: Preface, p. xiv, footnote 1 (p. 24 of the Cornell scan cu31924026424675)
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened; the text of p. 24 (= Preface p. xiv) and a 150-dpi render of the same page (saved as in the same folder) both show the passage: main text 'the sentences were numbered to facilitate reference, and all accents filled in as they occur in the original manuscript.1' and footnote 1 'As much may depend on the somewhat peculiar use made of those accents, the following is a copy of the author's own note on the subject :— Waar boven de syllabe een schuinsche linie (´) staat, dat die hard en lang moet uitgesprookken werden; desgeliks boven de g een liggende linie, aldus (ḡ) wyst aan die hard tegen de syde van de strot word uitgesprookken; en waar onder s op dese wyse een comma sta…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The 17th-century recorder marked, word by word, one syllable with an acute as 'hard and long' (i.e. a prominence/stress-cum-length mark); the source gives no rule for which syllable receives it, so placement must be read off the individual accented forms (which in the texts fall on various syllables, e.g. ma-acháchimit, Áttillono, arácho, Ma-ápapp'a). No positional generalization is stated in any source I could open.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the note is a key to diacritics, not a phonological rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Applies to written word forms in Vertrecht's Favorlang catechism texts (c.1650); accent is an orthographic per-word mark. The modern phonetic interpretation of this acute (Li 2003 'Notes on Favorlang'; Li 2019 sec. 4, pp. 6-10) was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: All accessible material concerns Favorlang, the 17th-century Dutch-recorded variety (Happart 1650, Vertrecht c.1650) that Glottolog/Blust treat as the older form of Babuza (babu1240; Joby 2026 likewise: 'une forme ancienne du babuza'). The 20th-century Babuza rememberer wordlists (Ogawa/Asai, in Tsuchida 1982) are a later stage of the same language; no separate glottocode for Favorlang at language level.
